title: What should you ask first in a growth strategy case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a growth strategy case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Growth cases are open questions, which makes them easy to ramble through. A little structure turns them into one of the friendlier case types.
body:
The first question to ask

Growth from where: revenue split by business unit?

How to build your structure

  • Organic: more from current customers, new segments or regions, new channels, new products
  • Inorganic: acquisitions, partnerships
  • Choose: size each option, rank by value and risk

The trap most people fall into

A list of ideas with no sizing or priority.

For the full tree, with every branch, read the growth strategy framework.

Two prompts to try

How can a mobile operator increase revenue per customer?

Show a model structure
  • Price: Plan prices, inflation-linked rises; Fewer discounts on renewal
  • Upgrade: Bigger data plans, 5G; Handset financing
  • Add services: Insurance, streaming bundles, home broadband; Family plans
  • Keep value: Churn of high-value customers; Stop customers moving to cheaper plans

Where to start: Upgrade and add services: price rises are fastest but risk churn.

The trap: Raising prices without checking churn.

Should a bubble-tea chain grow by franchising instead of opening its own shops?

Show a model structure
  • Economics for us: Fees and royalties vs own-shop profits; Capital needed
  • Speed: Shops opened per year each way; Our capacity to manage growth
  • Control: Quality and brand consistency; Choosing and supporting franchisees
  • Economics for franchisees: Franchisees' payback; Will good partners sign up?

Where to start: Economics for franchisees: if they can't make money, the model fails.

The trap: Looking only at our royalty income.

Turn a growth target into a gap to fill

A gym business has £50 million of annual revenue and wants to reach £60 million within two years. The £10 million gap is a 20% increase from today's base. Sketch a portfolio of levers, then assign reasonable sizes rather than listing ideas.

For example, opening five clubs generating £1 million each at maturity adds £5 million; a 5% price increase on £40 million of retained revenue adds up to £2 million before churn; selling personal-training packages to existing members might add £3 million. Together these bridge the target only if the assumptions are feasible and the revenue streams do not overlap.

Now ask what each lever does to profit and cash. New clubs consume capital and ramp up gradually; price rises can trigger cancellations; personal training requires qualified staff. Rank initiatives by incremental contribution, speed, execution risk and evidence. A credible growth case identifies where the ten million comes from and what must be true for it to arrive.
